title: The Impact of AI-Driven Tools on Student Writing Development: A Case Study From The CGScholar AI Helper Project
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how an AI-based writing feedback tool, CGScholar AI Helper, can support high school students’ writing development in English Language Arts. The study addresses a gap the authors identify in K-12 research on AI-supported writing, arguing that while AI writing tools are increasingly common, there is limited empirical evidence on their effects for school-age students. The authors are also interested in the design question of how generative AI can be recalibrated for education rather than used as unrestricted "AI in the wild." 

The intervention was a pilot implementation of CGScholar AI Helper, a web-based tool that gives AI-generated feedback on student writing using retrieval-augmented generation and teacher customization. The system was loaded with the teacher’s prompt, rubric, and source readings so that feedback would align with classroom expectations. Students submitted an initial draft of a 200-word comparative paragraph, received AI feedback tied to six rubric criteria, revised, received a second round of AI feedback, and then submitted a final version to the teacher. Data came from students’ initial and revised writing, a student focus group, a teacher post-survey, and researcher observations, analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis.

The study took place in one public high school in the Midwest United States in an 11th-grade ELA class serving a socioeconomically underserved community. Six students who consented from a class of twenty-three participated, along with one female ELA teacher. The implementation was embedded in normal classroom instruction around two assigned readings on Indigenous values and culture. The research team interviewed and trained the teacher and students on using the platform, and researchers were present during implementation to provide technical support and observe use.

The authors conclude that CGScholar AI Helper showed promise as a mediated AI writing support tool. Five of the six students improved on at least one rubric criterion after AI feedback, with gains especially in compare/contrast, composing claims, analysis, and introducing/connecting evidence. Student and teacher feedback suggested that the tool provided direct, actionable feedback and motivated revision, which the teacher described as otherwise difficult to elicit. At the same time, the paper notes that the AI feedback was sometimes too long and linguistically complex, and the authors emphasize that the tool is still under development. Overall, the study presents early, direct school-age evidence that rubric-aligned generative AI feedback may support revision and writing development in high school ELA, but only in a very small, single-site pilot without a comparison group.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small qualitative case study with one teacher and six consenting 11th-grade students, using draft comparisons, focus groups, observations, and a teacher survey but no control group, randomization, validated outcome instruments, or statistical testing. It provides direct K-12 evidence, but credibility is limited by the tiny sample and descriptive design.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising but unclear impact: most students improved on at least one writing criterion, but gains were uneven, some criteria showed no improvement, and no effect sizes were reported. Given the very small pilot sample of struggling writers in a low-income school, the evidence suggests possible modest benefit but not a quantified or clearly generalizable impact.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-calibrated AI writing feedback for 11th-grade ELA paragraph writing, using a RAG-based system and the teacher's rubric/materials to generate iterative feedback on compare/contrast, claims, evidence, conventions, and analysis.
Generative AI writing support embedded in the CGScholar platform to help students revise drafts through rubric-aligned textual feedback and optional follow-up clarification features.

finding.finding_summary: In this qualitative case study of 11th-grade ELA writing, 5 of 6 students improved on at least one rubric criterion after receiving CGScholar AI Helper feedback, and 1 student improved on three criteria. Improvements were reported in compare/contrast (3 students), composing defensible claims (2 students), analysis (2 students), and introducing/connecting evidence (1 student), while no improvements were identified for writing conventions or support of evidence; no standardized effect sizes or inferential statistics were reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-rubric-aligned AI ratings (0-4 stars) across six writing criteria, comparison of initial vs revised drafts, focus group feedback, teacher post-survey, and researcher observations

finding.finding_summary: Student focus group data and teacher post-survey suggested the tool increased motivation to revise and made revision feel more actionable. Students described the feedback as helpful, direct, and specific, and the teacher reported that the tool encouraged revision, though these findings are perception-based and derived from a very small sample without validated engagement scales.
finding.measure: Student focus group perceptions of helpfulness and revision support; teacher post-survey comments about motivation to revise
